Texans' Azeez Al-Shaair reportedly facing surgery after move to injured reserve

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (435 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Houston Texans are losing a key defensive piece for at least the next four games.
  • Over the next four weeks, Houston plays Indianapolis, the Baltimore Ravens, the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Washington Commanders.
  • In a recent development, al-Shaair, a Pro-Bowler in 2025, has dealt with the groin injury all year, missing a pair of games with it so far this season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Houston Texans are losing a key defensive piece for at least the next four games. Houston placed starting linebacker and team captain Azeez Al-Shaair on injured reserve, the team announced. Al-Shaair has been dealing with a groin injury that kept him out of Sunday's loss to the Cleveland Browns. The groin injury is significant enough that it requires surgery and he will likely miss more than four games, according to the Houston Chronicle.

Over the next four weeks, Houston plays Indianapolis, the Baltimore Ravens, the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Washington Commanders. The Texans then close the season with a four-game stretch in which they play the Jacksonville Jaguars, Philadelphia Eagles, Green Bay Packers and Tennessee Titans.

In a recent development, al-Shaair, a Pro-Bowler in 2025, has dealt with the groin injury all year, missing a pair of games with it so far this season. He has recorded 68 tackles, one tackle for loss, three quarterback hits and three passes defensed in seven games.

In Al-Shaair's absence, Jake Hansen will presumably see more snaps at linebacker (he played 66 of 68 defensive snaps against the Browns) while Henry To'oto'o will take over the green dot responsibilities of calling the defense, according to KPRC2.

It has been revealed that the Texans' defense as a whole has been one of the more disappointing units in the NFL in 2026, ranking 20th in yards allowed, 18th in points allowed, and 22nd in EPA per play, according to Tru Media. The Texans checked in first in yards, second in scoring and third in EPA per play a year ago, and were expected to again field one of the top defenses in the league this season after returning almost all of their key pieces.

Instead, Houston has struggled to contain opposing passing attacks this season, repeatedly leaking on the back end despite putting pressure on quarterbacks at an above-average rate. The Texans have also failed to force turnovers at the same rate as a year ago, with only 8.8% of opponents' drives resulting in a turnover (27th in the league) compared with 14.6% last season (fourth).

Those relative struggles have led the Texans to compile a 3-6 record despite C.J. Stroud and the offense showing significant year-over-year improvement. The Texans are now 2.5 games back of the No. 7 seed in the AFC and need to go on a strong run down the stretch of the season to have any hope of making the playoffs. And now, they'll likely have to do it without one of the leaders of their defense.

Taxes hurt: Breaking down an NFL player's weekly pay stub and where all the money goes

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (470 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you've ever wondered what an NFL player's paycheck looks like, we now know the answer thanks to Rashee Rice.
  • The paycheck offers a rare inside look into where all the money goes for an NFL player.
  • According to recent reports, like the rest of us, Rice has to pay taxes and he also has to pay his NFLPA dues.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you've ever wondered what an NFL player's paycheck looks like, we now know the answer thanks to Rashee Rice. The Chiefs wide receiver recently filed for bankruptcy, and as part of the court filing, he had to include a copy of his pay stub that he gets from the team each week.

The paycheck offers a rare inside look into where all the money goes for an NFL player. Rice is currently in the fourth and final year of a rookie deal that's paying him $1.635 million in base salary this year, but when it comes to his take-home pay, it's much more complicated than just looking at his base salary.

According to recent reports, like the rest of us, Rice has to pay taxes and he also has to pay his NFLPA dues. Not to mention, his paycheck is also being garnished to pay off several civil liabilities that he's facing.

Industry observers note that for the week of Oct. 19-25, Rice got paid $43,353.08, but he only got to take home a small portion of that.

Let's take a look at where the money went.

Here's a look at one of Rashee Rice's recent pay stubs from the Kansas City Chiefs (via his bankruptcy filing).$43,353 in weekly earnings- $19,570 for taxes/SS/Medicare- $9,117 for garnishments, union dues, and fines————= $14,665 in take-home payAs of October 25, Rice has… pic.twitter.com/dNjtBJaEVi.

It's certainly interesting to see how little Rice ends up taking home here.

After all the deductions were made, Rice's total net pay was $14,665.25. That means he only got to take home 33.9% of his paycheck. Most players don't have to deal with garnishments or fines, so let's take those out real quick. If Rice did NOT have to pay those two things, he still would have taken home only 52.7% of his paycheck ($22,860.96).

Another interesting thing about this pay stub is that you can see all the ways a player gets paid besides their base salary. For instance, Rice has been paid over $350,000 in performance pay along with a $75,000 workout bonus this year. Rice also earned $20,500 just for attending training camp. A player's salary only applies to games they play in, but they still do earn a stipend for training camp. Under the current CBA, veterans get paid $3,500 per week during training camp and this pay is equal for everyone, so Patrick Mahomes and Rice would make the same amount.

According to recent reports, although Rice is only making $43,000 per paycheck right now, that number will likely shoot up starting next year. The 26-year-old is in the final year of his rookie deal, and he'll definitely be cashing in this offseason, whether that's in free agency or signing an extension with the Chiefs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the NFL is flexing its scheduling freedom, moving the Week 12 Las Vegas Raiders at Cleveland Browns matchup from 1 p.m. ET to "Sunday Night Football." The Fresh England Patriots were originally scheduled to play the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium in prime time that week, but that matchup will now move to 4:05 p.m. ET.

Recent findings suggest that tennessee Titans at Jacksonville Jaguars, which was originally scheduled for 4:05 p.m. ET that week moves to 1 p.m. ET.

In a recent development, the Raiders-Browns matchup will feature Las Vegas's newest quarterback, Fernando Mendoza. The No. 1 overall pick took over after Vegas (4-6) sent Kirk Cousins to the Minnesota Vikings at the trade deadline last Tuesday, and Week 12 will mark the first prime-time matchup of his career. Mendoza completed 17 of 29 passes for 143 yards in his first career start on Sunday, which came in a 21-13 loss to the Seattle Seahawks.

As for the Browns, they moved to 6-4 last week following a remarkable comeback win over the Houston Texans. The 17-0 deficit Deshaun Watson and Co. overcame made it the second-largest comeback win at home in franchise history, while the Browns are now a perfect 4-0 in their home stadium for the first time since 1963. Cleveland right now holds the last wild-card spot in the AFC (No. 7 seed), behind the 6-3 Pittsburgh Steelers and 7-2 Denver Broncos.

The 5-5 Patriots are being flexed out of prime time following their disastrous 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Munich. The team reportedly fears that quarterback Drake Maye, who suffered a lower-leg injury early in the game, could be sidelined for an extended period of time. The injury could force last year's MVP runner-up to miss the remainder of the season. Newly introduced England's Week 12 opponent, the Chargers, actually just tallied their first win of the season on Monday night, defeating Jacoby Brissett's Baltimore Ravens, 23-20.

The NFL implemented this "flexible scheduling" rule in 2006. For "Sunday Night Football," they can flex up to two games between Weeks 5-10 and any week during Weeks 11-17.

Pressing Impossible: Amorim Loses to Hürzeler – MH

💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • Rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22.
  • Manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 21.01.2025 in den Kategorien Premier League mit 0 Kommentaren.

Rúben Amorim’s Manchester United faced Hürzeler’s Brighton on Matchday 22. While Manchester United focused on creating a pressing system that was as difficult as possible to bypass, Brighton once again showcased their incredibly challenging vertical play. You can find the tactical analysis of the match here.

Manchester United started in a nominal 3-2-4-1 formation, which transitioned into a classic 3-2-5 shape in possession and a 5-4-1 shape out of possession. Amorim initially placed particular emphasis on a pressing system that varied in height.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, Brighton began in a nominal 4-4-2 formation. In possession, Hürzeler’s trademark positional rotations, vertical runs, and decoy movements for effective vertical play were continuously on display. Accordingly, Brighton operated flexibly from a variety of shapes, such as 4-2-4, 3-1-4-2, 2-3-2-3, and more. This flexibility makes Brighton’s possession game almost impossible to define through formations alone.

Industry observers note that manchester United initially operated out of a 5-4-1 shape with varying defensive heights. This approach made it challenging for the opposition to play through, as different build-up phases required distinct patterns and connections. United’s central midfielders in the four-man line marked Brighton’s double pivot, Ayari and Baleba, man-to-man. The goal was to gain optimal control of Brighton’s central build-up play and apply immediate pressure whenever Brighton played through the middle.

Industry observers note that however, Brighton controlled the game during the first 10 minutes. Their holding midfielders positioned themselves close to the backline, creating a large gap between Manchester United’s five-man defensive line and the four-man midfield. This space was then exploited with various runs. When facing high pressing, left-back Estupiñán moved asymmetrically into the left half-space behind United’s first pressing block. This movement utilized the moment when Amad stepped out to press one of Brighton’s center-backs after bypassing Zirkzee.

United failed to adjust their pressing to this build-up variation throughout the match. As a result, this same pattern played a key role in Brighton’s build-up to the goal that made it 1-3.

It has been revealed that against Manchester United’s mid-block, Brighton’s strikers, Welbeck and João Pedro, alternated their runs into the large space between the lines, targeting the gaps. This repeatedly allowed Brighton to bypass United’s first pressing line.

Recent findings suggest that the 1-0 goal resulted from this setup, facilitated by a counter-movement. As striker Welbeck made a run into the space between the lines, he pulled his marker, De Ligt, a few steps out of the five-man backline. Simultaneously, winger Mitoma made a deep run into the space that opened up. De Ligt was caught in a dilemma between applying pressure and covering the depth. A long ball bypassed United’s entire pressing structure, leading to the goal.

Another reason for Brighton’s dominance in the first 10 minutes lay in their defensive work. United built up in a very positionally structured 3-2-4-1(/-5) shape. Brighton countered with a 4-4-2 in their high press and a 5-4-1 in their mid-block. With Minteh marking Diogo Dalot man-to-man on the flank, the two different defensive shapes emerged depending on Dalot’s positioning. Brighton’s two strikers also pressed United’s center-backs, Maguire and Yoro, on that side, applying intense pressure on the ball carriers on United’s left.

Sources indicate that on the other side, winger Mitoma positioned himself centrally when De Ligt had possession, cutting off the passing lane to Amad, who was positioned in the half-space. If the ball was played to full-back Mazraoui, Mitoma shifted out from the center to press, creating a cover shadow into the center. This approach effectively prevented United from creating any significant attacking threat on that flank as well.

Around the 10th minute, the game shifted, and Brighton’s dominance began to fade. This was due to several adjustments made by United. To reduce the pressure on the ball carrier on the left side, the highly press-resistant Bruno Fernandes started to drop deeper, while the full-backs pushed higher. The resulting 3-3-4 shape was difficult for Brighton to press, as full-back Veltman, or the half-space defender in the five-man backline, was pulled out, and the space in behind could be exploited by either full-back Dalot or striker Zirkzee. This led to more possession phases for United and fewer pressing phases from Brighton.

It has been revealed that another adjustment United made came from their 5-4-1 mid-block. The half-space defenders, De Ligt and Yoro, became much more aggressive in stepping out from the five-man backline to defend against the strikers making runs into the large space between the lines. This prevented Brighton’s strikers from turning after bypassing the first pressing block. To defend long balls to Mitoma, Mazraoui prioritized covering the space behind the advancing De Ligt. As a result, Brighton struggled to exploit the space between the lines and couldn’t progress as effectively into depth from their own possession.

In a recent development, additionally, Manchester United no longer pressed situationally from a 5-4-1 in a high press but instead switched to man-marking, with Zirkzee following the goalkeeper. This created much more pressure on the ball carriers for Brighton. Brighton also faced difficulties because the 5-4-1 system is much harder to break down than man-marking in a high press. This became evident in the sequence leading to the penalty goal. United suddenly switched to man-marking and forced the ball loss that preceded the penalty. United deservedly equalized.

After the 1-1, the game became more balanced. Brighton tried to break down the 5-4-1 mid-block, while United focused on their defensive game. When Manchester United switched to man-marking in the high press, Brighton continued to struggle and often lost possession. It is questionable why United didn’t press more boldly and high man-to-man during this phase to maintain better control of the game.

From Brighton’s perspective, a situational, more extreme overload at the moment of transition into high pressing—such as in the central space just behind the first pressing block—could have been a possible solution to challenge United’s man-marking, putting them in a dilemma between applying pressure and defending 1v1 on the wings.

Recent findings suggest that in possession, Brighton’s players frequently adjusted their positioning with small movements, creating newly introduced passing lanes, changing passing angles, and occupying spaces that forced the opponent into pressing reactions. Below, I have outlined the main advantages of three of the most frequently used shapes by Brighton against United, as well as the necessary reactions from the opponent.

Another factor that makes Brighton’s vertical play difficult to defend is the continuous variety of space-creating or counter-movement runs into depth. These consistently create dilemmas and positional problems for the defenders. Below, I have graphically illustrated some selected runs used against United:.

Despite Brighton’s possession game, Manchester United was able to prevent significant goal-scoring opportunities initially. From their 5-4-1 structure, the center-backs repeatedly defended aggressively, stepping out. Additionally, after bypassing the four-man midfield, it would drop back into position. This “recovery defense” made it difficult for Brighton to develop effective build-up play and exploit opened spaces. Furthermore, United’s players were well-prepared for potential through balls. In particular, the full-backs consistently intercepted balls played behind the defensive line.

It has been revealed that towards the end of the first half and into the second half, small (forced?) mistakes began to creep into United’s pressing. While the failure to step out with Ugarte in the man-marking high press in the 39th minute and the failure to step out with De Ligt in the space between the lines in the 38th minute went unpunished, the delayed step-out by Yoro led to Brighton’s deserved 1-2 at that point.

Especially in the second half, Brighton adapted to the man-marking high press by having center-backs step inside, breaking free from the cover shadow, when pressing the goalkeeper. This allowed them to find the open player in build-up, and Brighton lost possession less frequently.

Longer defensive phases in the mid-block for Manchester United followed. To break down this block, Brighton’s possession play became less positionally rigid. Much more frequently, certain zones were overloaded. In particular, the space between the lines and the half-spaces were repeatedly occupied by multiple players to create numerical superiority and apply pressure.

Industry observers note that united, on the other hand, struggled to create any significant goal-scoring chances. The high press could have been more effective with a brief orientation from the player pressing the goalkeeper to position the inward-dropping center-back into a cover shadow. From the 5-4-1 mid-block, too few dangerous ball recoveries and transition situations were created.

Sources indicate that even from their own possession, Manchester United created too few goal-scoring opportunities. When Amorim’s team did get chances, it was typically through a ball played behind the wide players of the five-man backline. At the moment the press was triggered (when Brighton stepped out to the outer center-back), the forward half-space player dropped deep, and the winger made a run in behind. However, the lack of other ways to break the press led to too much predictability in United’s possession play.

It has been revealed that as a result, the second half became more one-sided, with Brighton repeatedly pressing and trying to put United’s press under pressure. This ultimately succeeded, leading to a deserved 3-1 victory for Hürzeler’s team.

Recent findings suggest that amorim’s press, which was difficult to break down, was ultimately cracked by Hürzeler. It is questionable whether more frequent defensive pressing, alternating with situational man-marking high pressing, might have been a better approach against Brighton, in order to better tighten the space between the lines and the area behind the defense, making the game in depth more difficult. Despite a higher mid-block, Manchester United hardly created any dangerous transition situations. This is an area that needs improvement.

Hürzeler’s team, on the other hand, once again played highly attractive possession football. Frequent positional rotations, shifts in formations, overloads, and space-creating runs make Brighton’s possession game very enjoyable to watch. For the opponent, these constant shifts in zones over an extended period are incredibly difficult to defend. It is very likely that we will see more teams adopting similar principles in possession in the future.

It looked like this was going to be a night for “one of their own”, but Tottenham Hotspur’s latest big-money arrival, Sávio, stole the headlines to crank up the excitement at his fresh club.

Mikey Moore had set Spurs on their way to what proved a comfortable Carabao Cup success over Championship club Charlton Athletic and heard his name sung by the home fans.

But Sávio stepped off the substitutes’ bench to take the limelight with a late goal just a few days after completing his expensive switch from Manchester City, and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is demanding many more to come.

Sources indicate that “A perfect day for him,” noted De Zerbi. “His biggest improvement is to increase the number of goals. He is one of the best wingers, but the best wingers score many goals and I spoke with him two days ago, and we put the goal at 10-12 goals.

“We need 10-12 goals from the wingers. Last season, we suffered too much because the number of goals were not enough.”.

"What an introduction!"Sávio scores a brilliant goal on his Spurs debut! 👏 pic.twitter.com/WgmcfgeNpX.

A deal that could be worth as much as £85m, if add-ons are achieved, for Sávio certainly raised some eyebrows, but the Brazilian provided the perfect response by scoring just 11 minutes into his debut as a late substitute.

In the 82nd minute, Sávio cut in from the flank and scored with a shot past Charlton goalkeeper Tiernan Brooks. He and the Spurs crowd thought he had a second a few minutes later, but his shot hit Ben Davies on its way into the net and the defender was credited with the goal.

Three minutes after Moore’s opener, Dominic Solanke scored his first goal since March to offer a reminder of what he can still give De Zerbi, who is poised to welcome Omar Marmoush to Tottenham.

A place in the League Cup third round is at stake as Tottenham host Charlton in a London derby at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. The last competitive meeting between these sides came in the FA Cup back in January 2011, with Tottenham winning that game 3-0 at White Hart Lane. A then 19-year-old Andros Townsend made his debut that day and scored, with Jermain Defoe scoring a brace.

Tottenham’s Premier League campaign got off to the worst possible start as they lost 3-0 at Brentford last weekend. Tottenham have been very busy during this summer transfer window and that has continued this week. Savio (formerly Savinho) has arrived from Manchester City in a deal that could be worth £85m and the Brazilian could make his Tottenham debut tonight, having been registered in time.

“I think in attacking positions we need players capable one-on one, to create something, to create a chance to score,” Roberto De Zerbi said. “In terms of one-on-one, he [Savio] is one of the best players, especially since 2024. He can play on the right side, on the left side. I have known him from a long time, I spoke with him when he went to Manchester City. He is a big player for us.

“I do not know if I am the right man [to get the most out of Savio], but for sure he has to achieve. I think a player who is so good in one-on-one, so good at creating chances to score, to be complete, he has to score. If you analyse the other best wingers in the world, many of them, they score 10 to 15 goals per season. He has the qualities. Maybe his habits, he has to change habits, because he has to be focused on the assists, the one-on-one dribbling and also to score.”.

It has been revealed that omar Marmoush is closing in on an initial loan deal from Manchester City but that move is not complete and thus he is not available for Tottenham tonight. Micky van der Ven and Pedro Porro are both available having missed Tottenham’s loss at Brentford but the hosts are still without Xavi Simons, Pape Sarr, Dejan Kulusevski and Wilson Odobert.

Charlton have made the perfect start to their Championship campaign; a 2-1 home win over Derby was followed up by a 2-1 victory at recently-relegated West Ham. Nathan Jones’ side earned their place in the League Cup second round with a 3-1 win at Cheltenham in the first round.

According to recent reports, “We have to be very organised and very professional, they [Tottenham] are a top team,” Jones said. “They have a great manager and a brilliant group of players. They already had a Premier League squad and they have spent, what is reaching about, I do not know, £300 million or something like that. It is a wonderful test, we have to be right near our best and do both sides of the game very well. Of course, you want to test yourself against the best managers and you want to test yourself against the best teams. For us, this is not our priority, the Championship is our priority, but this is the next game and therefore it is the most vital.”.

You all remember the No. 1 rule about Fight Club, right? You don't talk about Fight Club.

There's a similar philosophy/mantra in the gambling space. You do not, under any circumstances, bring up the fact that you're on a heater, for fear of jinxing it. You simply don't acknowledge it, continue going about your business and pray that the good times keep rolling.

It has been revealed that with that in mind, I'm not going to tell you that I went 11-3 (ATS and straight-up) over the Week 10 slate, which included a near-perfect 4-1 ATS record in my five locks of the week. And I'm certainly not going to highlight that I'm currently on a 26-3 moneyline run over the past two weeks, along with a 7-3 ATS mark on my locks.

Industry observers note that again, I'm NOT telling you this. Why would I? Nope. All we need to do now is roll up our sleeves, pick up our lunch pail and keep it moving into Week 11. Because there isn't much else to talk about.

Note: Atlanta, Cleveland, Green Bay, Los Angeles (Rams), New England and Seattle are on the bye in Week 11.

All lines via DraftKings; All times ET.

I think Dallas is one of those teams that plays up or down to their opponent. So while it may have gone toe-to-toe with the 49ers last week, I wouldn't be surprised in the slightest to see the 1-8 Titans hang around. In fact, I'm betting they will. Tennessee is a respectable 3-1 ATS on the road this season. Conversely, AT&T Stadium hasn't been much of an advantage for Dallas, as it is 1-3 ATS at home.

In a recent development, over their last three games, the Titans offense has also been pretty solid, averaging 5.8 yards per play. That's the sixth-highest in the NFL over that stretch. A large part of that success has been thanks to the ground game, as they are averaging 5.4 yards per carry. The only team better than them is the 49ers, who just ran for 214 yards and three touchdowns against this Dallas defense in Week 10. The Cowboys' defense is showing no signs of improvement, as their 6.1 yards allowed per play are the sixth-highest in the NFL season. At the very least, the backdoor will be left wide open.

Projected score: Cowboys 30, Titans 23The pick: Titans +8.

In a recent development, los Angeles finally got a win, snapping an eight-game losing streak to start the season and an 11-game skid dating back to last year (including playoffs). This moment in the winner's circle, however, will be short-lived. With Geno Smith reportedly avoiding a major injury, that only strengthens my faith that the Jets will take down the Chargers on Sunday. I assume Smith plays, and with him under center, the Jets have been solid.

In a recent development, moreover, I thought Upcoming York's defense largely hung around against Buffalo last week before the wheels fell off in the second half. Justin Herbert is not Josh Allen, nor is Omarion Hampton James Cook, so the Jets' defense should be able to keep this offense in check for four quarters. New York also has the rest advantage after LA played in Baltimore on Monday night.

The Chargers have yet to record an ATS win (0-4) at home this season.

Projected score: Jets 24, Chargers 20The pick: Jets +3.5.

Recent findings suggest that the Jaguars are a freight train right now. Over their three-game winning streak, Jacksonville is averaging 38.3 points per game. For the season, they're averaging 6.0 yards per play (tied for fifth-highest in the NFL), a 46.8% conversion rate on third down (third-highest) and 8.7 yards per pass attempt (second-highest). Trevor Lawrence is playing at an MVP level, while running back Bhayshul Tuten is in the midst of a full-blown breakout. Over the winning streak, he's rushed for 221 yards and three touchdowns, while adding 80 yards and a touchdown on five receptions.

Meanwhile, Jacksonville's defense is about to get a boost this week as two of their trade deadline acquisitions (safety Jessie Bates III and defensive tackle Jordan Davis) are all set to make their debuts after Liam Coen gave them Week 11 off to get acclimated.

Sources indicate that while Newly introduced York does boast a defense that is allowing just 305.7 total yards per game this season (fifth-best in the NFL), the Jaguars feel like an entirely different animal to overcome. I also believe Jacksonville's defense, which is allowing 4.7 yards per play over the last three games (tied for fifth-lowest in the NFL), can contain a J.J. McCarthy-led Giants offense that still gives me pause.

When you look at the trends, the Jaguars have given bettors confidence to back them on the road this season. As the away team, Jacksonville is 3-1 ATS with a 9.5-point average margin of victory, the third-highest in the NFL.

Projected score: Jaguars 33, Giants 21The pick: Jaguars -6.

Fernando Mendoza actually played pretty well given the circumstances, in my opinion. The No. 1 overall pick was making his first career start against one of the toughest defenses in the NFL: the Seahawks. Naturally, he looked like a rookie quarterback at times, completing 17-of-29 for 143 yards, no touchdowns, and no interceptions. He was also sacked six times. That stated, he highlighted some flashes, including a touchdown run on his first possession of the afternoon. While Mendoza has a bright future in front of him, his baptism by fire will continue in Week 11 as he and the Raiders travel to Denver to face a Broncos team that was on the bye in Week 10.

Sources indicate that denver is 3-0 coming off a bye under head coach Sean Payton, and its pass rush could prove to be the difference in this game and keep Las Vegas outside of the number. This season, Denver is second in the NFL in pressures (159) and tied for the ninth-most sacks in the league (26), according to TruMedia. At home, this feels like a recipe for Mendoza to be under siege early and often, allowing Bo Nix and the Broncos offense to simply take advantage of what has been a poor Vegas defense. Coming into Week 11, the Raiders are tied for the most points per game allowed (28.9) in the NFL.

Projected score: Broncos 27, Raiders 16The pick: Broncos -10.

There are a lot of substantial spreads this week, so we're naturally going to see some teams creep through the back door. I think Fresh Orleans could be one of them. The Saints are tied for the second-most pass attempts per game (38.1) in the NFL this season. That number jumps to a league-high 39.5 when they're on the road. That should only continue in this matchup against Chicago as they try to keep up with Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams on the other side.

The Saints' passing attack is also getting a midseason boost with the return of first-round rookie Jordyn Tyson. Over the first two games of his career, the No. 8 overall pick has looked like the real deal, including an 11-catch, 80-yard outing last week in the loss to Carolina. Paired with Chris Olave, that's a nice one-two punch for Tyler Shough to get us to a cover. Speaking of covers, that's all Newly introduced Orleans has done this season, as they're the only team in the NFL without an ATS loss on the road so far in 2026 (3-0).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Heading into Week 11, the NFL playoff race is supposed to be heating up, but it might actually be cooling down, at least in the AFC.

Industry observers note that several things happened in Week 10 that make it feel like the AFC playoff field might be set. For one, Drake Maye went down with a potentially season-ending injury, and because of that, the Patriots (5-5) are now a long shot to make the playoffs. Also, the Browns pulled off a stunning comeback win over the Texans, putting Cleveland in firm control of a wild card spot.

According to recent reports, according to our projection, the AFC's seven-team playoff field is all but set. So who's projected to get in? Glad you asked.

It has been revealed that to help us figure that out, we had our analytics expert, Stephen Oh, simulate the rest of the 2026 season. There are 122 games left on the regular-season schedule, along with 13 playoff games, and Oh simulated all of them. Not only did he project all eight division winners and the 14 playoff teams, but he also crowned a Super Bowl champion.

With that in mind, let's get to the projections. And just as a reminder, we're projecting what the NFL playoff field will look like at the end of the season. This is NOT the current playoff standings.

It has been revealed that the biggest win in Week 10 was probably the Browns' wild comeback victory over the Texans. With Cleveland's win, the Browns are now projected to get the seventh seed in place of Houston, who was there last week.

Here's the projected AFC playoff field (with each team's current record):  1. Bills (8-1) -- AFC East champion 2. Jaguars (7-2) -- AFC South champion 3. Bengals (7-2) -- AFC North champion 4. Chiefs (7-2) -- AFC West champion 5. Broncos (7-2) 6. Steelers (6-3) 7. Browns (6-4) JUST MISSED: Patriots (5-5), Texans (3-6).

BREAKDOWN: According to our projection, the AFC playoff field is basically wrapped up. That's right, we're only in Week 11, but our model feels pretty strongly that these will be your seven playoff teams. The model has given up on the Patriots because they just lost Drake Maye, the Ravens have been left for dead after losing to the Chargers, and even if the Texans somehow rebound to get to 10 wins, they're in a spot where they would lose almost any tiebreaker (they've already lost to the Bills, Bengals and Browns, so the head-to-head tiebreaker is out the window). They do play the Steelers in Week 13, and at this point, that's essentially a must-win game for Houston.

The addition of Kirk Cousins has caused a ripple effect in the NFC North. After watching Cousins lead the Vikings to a win over the Packers in Week 10, our computer now projects the Vikings will win the NFC North (the Lions were projected to win it before the Cousins trade).

Sources indicate that here's the projected NFC playoff field (with each team's current record):  1. 49ers (8-1) -- NFC West champion 2. Vikings (7-2) -- NFC North champion 3. Giants (5-3-1) -- NFC East champion 4. Buccaneers (3-6) -- NFC South champion 5. Lions (7-2) 6. Bears (7-2) 7. Seahawks (6-4)  JUST MISSED: Packers (6-4), Rams (6-4).

Sources indicate that the most interesting part of the NFC projection is that we have the Packers and Rams both reaching 10 wins but still missing the postseason. To add insult to injury, our projection has the Buccaneers (8-9) and Giants (8-8-1) both finishing at .500 or below, yet still getting in as a division winner.

AFC breakdown: The AFC wild card round would be must-see TV with two huge divisional showdowns. The Bengals just destroyed the Steelers in Week 10, and the computer has them once again winning in the postseason. The juiciest game in the AFC would come in Kansas City, where the Chiefs would edge the Broncos in a thriller. As for the other game, the computer is predicting a short playoff run for Cleveland.

In a recent development, NFC breakdown: We didn't see a single home team lose in the AFC wild card round, but in the NFC, things are much different, with the home teams going a combined 1-2. The NFC North sends three teams through to the divisional round, becoming just the fourth division in the Super Bowl era to pull that off. This round also sees the elimination of the Seahawks, which means the NFL will crown a newly introduced champion.

Sources indicate that AFC breakdown: Our projection has the Bills beating the Chiefs, but I'll believe it when I see it. On paper, the Bills might have the better overall roster, but that never seems to matter when these two teams meet in the postseason. Patrick Mahomes is 4-0 all-time against Josh Allen in the playoffs, and if our projection is right, Allen's drought will finally end here. As for the other game, the Jags beat the Bengals in Cincinnati earlier this year, and our projection has the Jags earning the win again in Jacksonville.

It has been revealed that NFC breakdown: We get total chaos in the NFC with two crazy games that end up going down to the wire. Kirk Cousins leads the Vikings to their first NFC title game appearance since 2017 while the 49ers edge the Bears in a thriller.

If you're scoring at home, we are now down to four teams: three teams that have never won a Super Bowl (Bills, Jaguars and Vikings) and one team that hasn't won a Super Bowl in over 30 years (the 49ers' last title came in 1994).

We've been doing a projection every week since the start of the season, and here's a look at the projected Super Bowl each week.

In a recent development, for the FIRST time all season, our computer has projected the same Super Bowl matchup for TWO straight weeks. The Bills have been projected to win the Super Bowl for four straight weeks and that's mostly because the computer loves them. Our model gives the Bills an 18.27% chance of winning it all, which is incredibly high, especially given that no other team is above 11%.

#26798. Sorting 9 struggling franchises into tiers, from hopeless to hopeful: When will Jets end drought?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1378 w)

Sorting 9 struggling franchises into tiers, from hopeless to hopeful: When will Jets end drought?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1378 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The last time the Upcoming York Jets made the playoffs was all the way back in 2010.
  • Reasons for hope exist inside most of these downtrodden teams who have waited at least three years for a return to the Super Bowl hunt.
  • For the franchises that lack those puzzle pieces, however, the outlook is far bleaker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The last time the Upcoming York Jets made the playoffs was all the way back in 2010. Their 15-year postseason drought is the longest in franchise history and by far the longest active streak in the NFL. The Atlanta Falcons own the second-longest run without a playoff berth at eight years, and nine different teams own droughts of at least three seasons. Through 10 weeks in 2026, a couple of those squads appear poised to snap their dry spells. But others are destined to watch the postseason from home yet again.

Reasons for hope exist inside most of these downtrodden teams who have waited at least three years for a return to the Super Bowl hunt. Emerging or solidified franchise quarterbacks, superstar talent and renowned coaches are the best foundational pieces to own on the road back to competitiveness.

For the franchises that lack those puzzle pieces, however, the outlook is far bleaker.

Below are the nine teams with the longest postseason droughts sorted into tiers from hopeful to hopeless.

The two most aggressive sellers at the trade deadline are in the earliest stages of a rebuild. Yes, even the Titans, who started theirs back in 2023.

Sources indicate that tennessee whiffed on their first swing at a franchise quarterback when Will Levis did not work out, which essentially reset the clock on their rebuild. Then they made a second coaching change in two years by bringing in Robert Saleh, which amounted to another overhaul. The Jeffery Simmons and Amani Hooker trades this month moved a franchise legend and the NFL's most prolific defender at forcing interceptions and set the roster's talent back again. All the while, the product on the field has not improved one bit. Since Mike Vrabel's exit in 2023, the Titans have not won more than three games in a season. They are on pace for two this year. And while there are fun young weapons on the offense, it is still unclear whether Cam Ward is the answer at quarterback.

The Colts gutted their roster save for Jonathan Taylor, Sauce Gardner and Daniel Jones, and more moves could be on the way in the offseason. They have an opening at general manager, might be in search of a new coach in a couple of months, are devoid of talent at wide receiver and probably need to change things up at quarterback considering Jones' dreadful production in his first year back from a torn Achilles. This will get worse before it gets better. And on top of all that, they do not have a 2027 first-round pick.

Geno Smith and recently traded Jacoby Brissett are classic veteran bridge quarterbacks whose job is to keep their teams somewhat competitive until they draft their replacements. The Cardinals already moved on from Brissett and are taking a look at the future with Carson Beck, and he did not look the part of a future starter in his debut in Week 10. Both them and the Jets will shop for a signal-caller in the draft.

The quarterback Arizona selects will have an elite receiving tight end in Trey McBride, which will give that incoming rookie a premier safety valve as he gets his feet wet. If and when Jeremiyah Love gets and stays healthy, there is tremendous upside at running back, too. The Cardinals need to upgrade their receiving unit to aid their next quarterback, though. Decisions await on the other side of the ball, where Budda Baker and Josh Sweat remain locked in as two veteran leaders after the Cardinals elected to keep them at the trade deadline.

Sources indicate that years of mediocrity and the NFL's longest playoff drought helped the Jets stockpile young talent, so the quarterback they select might inherit an even better situation than the one in Arizona. The offensive skill positions are flush with rising standouts and established stars. David Bailey is a tremendous building block for the defense as the league leader in forced fumbles with five and a havoc-wreaker with 7.5 sacks as a rookie. The Jets just need to finally hit on a quarterback and ace the coaching hire that feels destined to come with Aaron Glenn on perhaps the hottest seat in the NFL.

Each of these teams own the same blueprint: A developing young quarterback who may be their long-term solution, at least one offensive star or superstar and enough promising or established tertiary weapons to keep them out of the league's basement.

Sources indicate that the Saints have trailed at some point in all 26 games of Kellen Moore's tenure. That appalling reality does not instill much confidence that he is the right man for the job. A porous defense is largely to blame for this year's issues, as it ranks 29th in yards allowed per game, 26th in scoring and 23rd in EPA per play allowed. Between that and the musical chairs the Saints have played at running back, the positives that continue to come out of Tyler Shough and his receivers only go so far.

Las Vegas was among the most pleasant surprises of the season's first half, although the luster wore off in the weeks leading up to the Kirk Cousins trade. It was obvious in the first few weeks of the season that Klint Kubiak was an excellent hire and that if Fernando Mendoza delivers on his promise as the No. 1 pick, it will not take long for the Raiders to make noise. Brock Bowers ought to aid Mendoza's development, but they are still in desperate need of wide receiver help and must build around Maxx Crosby on defense.

In a recent development, the combination of Bijan Robinson and Drake London is a legitimate championship-caliber duo that the Falcons hope does not go to waste. Even some locked-in playoff contenders would gladly take Atlanta's skill position weapons over their own. The key for coach Kevin Stefanski is to mold Michael Penix Jr. into at least an upper-half-of-the-league quarterback and field a defense strong enough to maximize the elite playmaking ability on the more loaded side of the ball. That latter task got a little tougher when the Falcons traded Jessie Bates III, though.

Jaxson Dart's season-ending injury in Week 2 will always make this a "what could have been" season for the Giants. How much they accomplish in the second half of the campaign will determine how much excitement will exist for Year 2 of the John Harbaugh era when Dart returns to action.

Harbaugh is a strong candidate for Coach of the Year and continues to make the most of a rough situation without his starting quarterback — so much so that the Giants, even on the heels of a disappointing loss, are in the driver's seat in the NFC East. He could be set for a lengthy tenure in New York if everything goes according to proposal. He and Joe Schoen will work together to add even more talent to this roster after the latter turned in a couple of highly fruitful drafts and loaded the squad with some of the league's most exciting young players like Malik Nabers, Abdul Carter and Arvell Reese.

It has been revealed that this version of the Bengals is the one the franchise had to have envisioned when Joe Burrow led his 2022 team to the Super Bowl. It just took a few years to manifest. Now that it has arrived, Cincinnati might not just get back to the Super Bowl; it could win it.

Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase, Tee Higgins and Chase Brown were never the problem. All the reasons behind the three-year playoff drought had to do with either injuries or the defense. In 2026, the stars have stayed healthy, and the commitment to fixing the defense has paid off. The Bengals spent all offseason trading for, signing and drafting impact players on their weaker half of the roster. Dexter Lawrence. Boye Mafe. Bryan Cook. Each of them, along with others, has taken the unit to a fresh level. Consistency still lacks a bit, but the highs are higher than at any other point during the Burrow era. If the defense peaks down the stretch, nobody will be able to keep up with the third-highest-scoring team in football.

#26797. Latest Update: Between a Lack of Stability and Connection Issues

Latest Update: Between a Lack of Stability and Connection Issues

📅 25 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2784 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spielverlagerung

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren.
  • Tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short.
  • Christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

von Next Generation am 25.01.2025 in den Kategorien Europa League mit 0 Kommentaren.

Tottenham Hotspur and TSG Hoffenheim disappoint on Thursday evening in Sinsheim, with Hoffenheim showing promising adjustments in the second half but still falling short. It was a match defined by approaches and ambivalence, as both teams displayed glimpses of potential but lacked the necessary consistency and presence. (MX).

Christian Ilzer and TSG Hoffenheim were under pressure on the penultimate matchday of the UEFA Europa League: Only a win would keep their theoretical chance of direct progression alive. The Austrian coach opted for a 4-2-2-2 formation. Oliver Baumann performed as usual as the goalkeeper, with Akpoguma and Nsoki forming the center-back duo, flanked by Jurásek on the left and Kadeřábek on the right. The double pivot consisted of Stach and Becker, while Bischof – who will soon join FC Bayern – and Hložek were deployed in the half-spaces. Up front, Morstedt and Kramarić played as a dual-striker pair.

On the opposite side, there was also significant pressure on Ange Postecoglou and Tottenham. Domestically, the team was in a difficult situation, and in the Europa League, a win was necessary to keep their chances of progressing in their own hands for the following week. The Spurs lined up in a 4-3-3 formation, with Austin in goal. Dragusin and Davies formed the central defensive pairing, while Gray and Porro occupied the full-back roles. In midfield, Maddison, Bentancur, and the young Bergvall played as central figures. The attacking line consisted of Kulusevski, Richarlison, and Son.

Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 Pressing System.

The Hoffenheim pressing structure without the ball was primarily based on a 4-4-2 formation, which Ilzer had successfully used in recent weeks and also in Graz for midfield pressing. In this formation, Bischof and Hložek played as wide players, while Moerstedt and Kramarić formed the first pressing line. The ball-near striker didn’t press the ball-carrying center-back directly, but rather in a looser manner. The main focus was on controlling the diagonal dribbles of Dragusin and Davies and blocking the diagonal passing lanes into the center. Additionally, the far-side striker often took on the task of marking Bentancur, the central defensive midfielder.

Recent findings suggest that A key characteristic of Ilzer’s approach was also that the strikers often moved wide from their diagonal pressing movements, putting more pressure on the width and preventing backward passes more effectively. This approach indirectly highlighted how crucial compactness is for Ilzer’s system. Without tight distances between the lines, it was difficult for the strikers to press effectively and create double pressure. In situations where compactness was not ensured, such as in some midfield pressing moments, unfavorable 1v1 situations arose that significantly diminished the advantage of the system, as the player could directly engage in a 1v1 duel instead of a 1v2 situation with the pressing striker.

It has been revealed that the attempt to block diagonal movements by the pressing striker inevitably led to a drawback: Tottenham was increasingly forced to play wide. Here, Hoffenheim highlighted some ambivalence. Tottenham frequently positioned their full-backs in half-space, forcing Bischof and Hložek to track them. The problem, however, was that the width, which should have been covered by the outer midfielders in the 4-4-2 system, was insufficiently secured. This created patterns that became an increasing challenge for Hoffenheim.

Tottenham’s Width-Based Strategy.

Postecoglou likely recognized the importance of exploiting width in deeper spaces ahead of the match, aiming to establish patterns that would facilitate effective use of the width.

The half-space players in the 2-3-2-3 system, Bergvall and Maddison, made dynamic movements into the wider areas, made possible by Hoffenheim’s first pressing line. The goal was to create shorter connections for the center-backs to progress into the wide areas. Complementing this, the full-backs, Porro and Gray, deliberately positioned themselves to bind Hoffenheim’s wide players, Hložek and Becker, in the half-space, thereby providing more space and time for Tottenham’s wide players.

Hoffenheim responded solidly, especially through clear handovers. The central midfielder, in this case, Becker, would situationally take over the full-back, allowing the wide player to shift into the wide areas. However, Maddison could have made more of the side pressing angle from Hložek in some situations. By turning directly forward, he could have bypassed the pressure from the first line and, alongside Son, created a 2v1 against Kadeřábek. This option, however, was rarely utilized.

Son repeatedly dropped deeper, pulling Kadeřábek out of the defensive line, but this often led to a lack of consistent height occupation for Tottenham. As a result, many progression opportunities—especially down the left side—remained ineffective. Although Hoffenheim’s attempts to push the full-backs wide created space in the half-space, Porro did exploit these opportunities successfully in a few instances, but overall, he did so too rarely to create sustained attacking dynamics. Richarlison could also have moved into these spaces more frequently in the opening phase to strengthen the attacking rhythm.

According to recent reports, in general, one positive aspect was the consistent use of layoff play on the right build-up side, with Porro tucking inside. Bergvall, who positioned himself wide, showed excellent awareness of the game situations under pressure from the opposition. He quickly recognized that Stach was marking Porro loosely, which allowed Bergvall to frequently find Porro in the center. This situation was well exploited, leading to effective one-two patterns and significantly supporting the build-up structure on the right side.

Tottenham’s Half-Space Positioning and Defensive Weaknesses.

In a recent development, A recurring pattern for Tottenham was the positioning of the half-space players. They often remained in their usual positions, staying in the half-space rather than fully occupying the width, but frequently aligning with Bentancur, which resulted in a 2-5-3 system. This setup was often accompanied by deeper, but wide, movements from Kulusevski and Son.

Industry observers note that due to the binding of Hložek and Bischof by Tottenham’s half-space players, Hoffenheim found it difficult to transfer the ball into the wide areas in a ball-oriented manner. Instead, they were forced to play out through the full-backs, which revealed weaknesses in the ball-oriented shifting of their defensive line. This resulted in large gaps, which Tottenham sought to exploit through quick vertical movements, especially in the half-space. Bergvall in particular pushed forward several times, but tended to do so too swiftly, making it difficult for Kulusevski to receive the ball in these patterns. Nsoki, however, defended man-to-man and was able to largely isolate Bergvall’s movements.

Overall, Kulusevski struggled, particularly under the pressure exerted by Kramarić’s pressing, which intensified the pressure. Return passes to the defensive line were consistently denied. Kulusevski had noticeable difficulty, especially with his first touch, to escape these tight situations.

It has been revealed that an additional factor was that Kulusevski was often forced to turn using his weaker foot. Combined with the double pressure from Hoffenheim, this led to significant concerns in ball control, making it difficult for him to find Bergvall diagonally in the half-space.

2-0 and 50% Possession at Halftime.

By the end of the first half, Hoffenheim had only partially been able to capitalize on Tottenham’s initial struggles. What stood out most was that the characteristic pressing through the strikers became less frequent, as Bentancur shifted closer to the ball, increasingly binding the ball-near striker, which led to a noticeable decrease in the intensity of the overall pressing. This change allowed Tottenham to play more return passes and initiate new build-up attempts without being under constant pressure.

Additionally, Son was regularly placed in 1v1 situations in the final third towards the end of the half, which naturally created dynamics—helped by some unfortunate defensive actions from Kadeřábek. Furthermore, Richarlison and Maddison often found space in the in-between lines. The large gaps in Hoffenheim’s 4-4-2 system offered Tottenham the opportunity to target these players and create additional dynamics in their offensive play.

Industry observers note that despite the early lead and a 2-0 score before halftime, Tottenham had just over 50% possession against Hoffenheim by the end of the first half. This surprisingly low figure was partly due to the disjointed nature of the game: many ball losses and fouls characterized the match, with Hoffenheim particularly focusing on physical intensity in the half-space. Additionally, Tottenham demonstrated general problems with coordination and connections between players. Notably, the lack of ball flow was apparent: passes often went astray, and there were difficulties with the first touch— a crucial disadvantage, especially for a style of play that heavily relies on width and time advantages along the sidelines.

Industry observers note that through the 2-5-3 (or 2-3-5 in the final third), Tottenham also revealed significant weaknesses in their counter-pressing. This was primarily due to ball losses occurring frequently in the wide areas, with surrounding players often moving away from the ball. As a result, there was a lack of necessary ball concentration near the ball, making an effective, pressing-oriented counter-pressing difficult to execute, forcing Tottenham to frequently fall back instead.

In Hoffenheim’s build-up play under Ilzer in the first half, a clear game plan was evident: instead of a short build-up, they focused almost entirely on long ball distribution.

In a recent development, in principle, the team played out of a 2-3-5 formation, with Kadeřábek and Jurasec positioned more centrally in the second build-up line, but occasionally shifting wide. Stach operated centrally between them, while Becker frequently advanced from the back line and occasionally dropped into the intermediate spaces.

The extreme overload of the back line was closely linked to Max Moerstedt, who acted as the target player. The striker regularly drifted to the left side, positioning himself close to Porro in order to receive long balls. Around him, three players—usually Bischof, Kramarić, and another teammate—positioned themselves to ensure that the area around the ball was well occupied.

The central issue with this approach, however, was the overly tight positioning of the players around Moerstedt. The second balls often ended up in more distant zones (green zone), areas that Tottenham could access well from their 4-4-2/5-3-2 structure. Notably, the wide players Son and Kulusevski frequently shifted excellently into these spaces, leading to dangerous counter-attacking situations.

It has been revealed that both goals conceded in the first half resulted from ball losses in these zones, which Hoffenheim failed to protect effectively. Tottenham’s quick transitions and precise vertical play made the problems with the long ball distribution clearly visible.

In general, Moerstedt had a rather unsuccessful day with the long balls. While the balls were often played back towards Baumann intentionally, these passes frequently lacked precision. Additionally, both Porro and Drăgușin were extremely dominant in aerial duels on this occasion.

Recent findings suggest that sending Moerstedt into an aerial duel within a densely populated zone also assumes that the team maintains a certain depth behind the target player. However, Hoffenheim failed to establish this depth adequately, resulting in second balls rarely being secured in the deeper areas.

According to recent reports, towards the end of the half, Hoffenheim shifted its strategic focus from long balls to short build-up plays, which were mainly initiated on the right side. Kadeřábek positioned himself increasingly wide, which proved effective, as his direct opponent Son, starting from a half-space position, had to cover a long pressing distance and often arrived too late. This allowed Kadeřábek to receive the ball.

Sources indicate that from there, Hoffenheim attempted to play quickly into depth to Hložek or Becker. However, Tottenham effectively defended this option through consistent man-marking. Becker’s dropping movements were frequently neutralized by Maddison’s covering shadow in the half-space, while Stach was largely covered by Richarlison, limiting the connections into the center significantly.

In the second half, Hoffenheim continued with this approach, but increasingly operated from a 2-3-4-1 formation, while Tottenham defended in a 4-1-4-1. The full-backs positioned themselves in extreme width early in the build-up phases to maximize the pressing distances of their direct opponents. This approach remained effective: With clean first touches, Hoffenheim occasionally managed to beat their opponents with dribbles.

The biggest difference from the first half lay in the subsequent movements from wide positions. Unlike in the first half, Hoffenheim refrained from structurally overloading the last line. The focus shifted towards deeper positioning to create diagonal passing options. This allowed Hoffenheim to either play directly behind Tottenham’s defensive line or use the space in between, where Hložek was frequently available for a pass.

In a recent development, there were also frequent rotations, for example between Bischof and Becker, which created additional dynamism. Kramaric often dropped into the defensive midfield space, allowing for the resolution of the isolation of that space by Richarlison, as Tottenham didn’t follow these wide runs in their man-marking system. This allowed Kramaric to distribute the ball on several occasions.

Sources indicate that A positive aspect was that Akpoguma kept up with Kadeřábek’s wide movements, constantly offering a return pass option. Meanwhile, Stach often dropped deeper to cover space for counter-attacks—a lesson learned from the first half. Since Tottenham struggled to defend the width consistently, the pressing became deeper, and Hoffenheim’s pressure steadily increased.

Although Hoffenheim almost completely stopped playing long balls, the wide fullbacks presented themselves as viable options for diagonal switches, which were frequently sought. Sometimes Bischof also dropped wide to be available for these passes. These passes were mostly successful, as they were played into open spaces rather than into congested areas. Moreover, the 2-3-4-1 formation allowed for much better access to second balls due to the increased midfield presence.

For Tottenham, however, it remained a similar game to the first half. They still faced significant problems with the opponent behind them and technical difficulties in their ball retention play. Solanke added a bit more depth in the forward position, while Moore displayed more dribbling strength on the left wing. Despite some good individual actions, the problem areas—particularly in the final third from the very static 2-3-5—were still largely unresolved. Hoffenheim, on the other hand, simply had a better ball possession structure and dominated the game with nearly 61% possession. The counter-pressing issues ultimately led to Hoffenheim’s 1-2 goal.

Towards the end of the match, Ilzer switched to a 2-4-4 system with double-wide wingers, while Spurs also switched to a 4-1-4-1 formation, defending much wider. They tried to directly cut off the connection to the wide fullbacks, which they succeeded in doing effectively. Once they were bypassed, however, the fullbacks advanced well. The central players were now more tightly marked, following movements towards the ball. It wasn’t until Moore failed to notice Kadeřábek’s off-the-ball runs in the 88th minute that Hoffenheim managed to break free on the wing and score the 2-3 goal.

Overall, Tottenham’s initially wider setup made the half-space more accessible, which Hoffenheim repeatedly attempted to exploit. However, Moerstedt and Kramaric found few solutions against Tottenham’s well-defending center-backs. Several of these situations led to relieving counter-attacks for Tottenham, which were also the most dangerous for them in the second half. Especially towards the end of the match, as Solanke and Lankshear pressed for ball recoveries, Tottenham could rapidly play vertically forward after regaining possession. Maddison’s dribbling pace was also frequently on display in these moments. It was clear that the fact Tottenham was ahead and Hoffenheim needed to win played into their hands.

Recent findings suggest that the conclusion is ambivalent. Both teams are going through a difficult phase, which was reflected in the match—many fouls, turnovers, and long balls shaped the game. It was not a particularly convincing display from two teams that, in terms of personnel and concept, should be doing better. Both sides were often forced into wide areas or specific zones, which fragmented the combination play in the final third and lacked the necessary dynamism.

However, there were still glimpses of solid, familiar approaches, particularly from Hoffenheim, though the team still lacks the presence and stability required to compete against stronger opponents. As Ilzer highlighted in the post-match press conference: “We’ve learned that we need to be more stable to get the right results. In duels man against man, we lacked something. Still, you can see we can play really good football. We ruin a good game for ourselves when we make such simple mistakes. It was too easy for the opponent.”.

Postecoglou’s team also indicated deficiencies, especially in ball movement, presence in the final third, and intensity without the ball. Ultimately, the team that managed to relieve pressure better came out on top, while the other, had they played the second half like the first, might have seen a different outcome.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arsenal will host old nemesis José Mourinho’s Real Madrid in the league phase of the Champions League.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal will host old nemesis José Mourinho’s Real Madrid in the league phase of the Champions League.

Mourinho, the former Chelsea, Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur manager, will return to London to resume hostilities against last season’s beaten finalists.

Other reunions from Thursday’s draw include Manchester City travelling to Barcelona, to whom they last week sold Rodri, and Liverpool visiting Inter Milan, who have signed Curtis Jones.

Sources indicate that arsenal will also travel to Harry Kane’s Bayern Munich, while United will host the Germans as well on their Champions League return in a repeat of the legendary 1999 final. Michael Carrick’s side will also visit Cesc Fàbregas’s Como.

Mourinho last managed at the Emirates Stadium in March 2021, barely a month before his sacking by Spurs.

This season is the third under the new format, with a league phase instead of a group stage, and Uefa has confirmed that fixtures that have taken place in the league phase of the two previous seasons cannot be repeated this time around.

The teams will be split into four pots of nine, based on “club coefficient rankings”, with defending champions Paris St-Germain automatically named as the top seed.

Liverpool, Manchester City and Arsenal will be among the teams joining the Parisians in pot one, while the two remaining English teams, Manchester United and Aston Villa, will be in pot two.

For example, Liverpool cannot host Real Madrid in the league phase this term after welcoming the 15-time European champions to Anfield at this stage of the previous two campaigns. Andoni Iraola’s side could, however, travel to the Bernabeu for an away meeting with Madrid.

The league phase will kick off on 8 September and will be wrapped up after all teams play at the same time on 27 January. The top eight teams of the league phase progress to the last 16 automatically, while teams that finish between ninth and 24th will be forced to navigate a play-off tie to reach the knockout stages.

#26791. Barbra Banda talks a 2021 in which she rose to global prominence and the future
